props.title: Two Can Play That Game
props.initialSlug: A woman's guide to controlling her man backfires

sections.content: **Two Can Play That Game** (2001) revolutionized the Black romantic comedy genre by breaking the fourth wall years before **Fleabag** (2016) made it trendy. Vivica A. Fox's Shante Smith speaks directly to viewers, teaching her rules for keeping men in line - a device that influenced films like **Think Like a Man** (2012) and **What Men Want** (2019). The film's sharp commentary on dating power dynamics and gender warfare resonated particularly well with urban audiences, while maintaining broad appeal through its universal relationship insights.

sections.content: The early 2000s marked a golden age for Black romantic comedies that tackled class dynamics within the African American community. **The Brothers** (2001) and **Brown Sugar** (2002) explored successful Black professionals navigating love, while **Deliver Us from Eva** (2003) continued the battle-of-the-sexes theme with LL Cool J and Gabrielle Union's electric chemistry. These films shared DNA with **Two Can Play That Game** in their sophisticated portrayal of upper-middle-class Black characters rarely seen in mainstream cinema of the era.

Director Mark Brown's approach influenced a wave of relationship comedies that mixed direct audience address with ensemble storytelling. **Think Like a Man** (2012) borrowed heavily from this template, using Steve Harvey's relationship book as a framing device similar to Shante's rules. The format proved so successful that it spawned variations like **He's Just Not That Into You** (2009) and **What to Expect When You're Expecting** (2012), though few matched the original's sharp wit and cultural specificity. sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond its immediate era into contemporary romantic comedies. **Girls Trip** (2017) and **Little** (2019) follow successful Black female professionals while maintaining the humor and friendship dynamics that made **Two Can Play That Game** resonate. Modern films like **Insecure** (2016-2021) and **The Lovebirds** (2020) continue exploring similar themes of relationship power dynamics and career-focused Black women, though with updated sensibilities for current audiences.
